sentences.text: Tiktaalik roseae is the only species in a monospecific genus of extinct lobe-finned fish that lived approximately 375 million years ago.
Specimens of this animal ranged in total length from 1.25 to 2.75 meters, with the largest known fossils reaching 2.75 meters and having lower jaws that measured 31 centimeters.
It possessed a low, flat skull shape more similar to a salamander than to most fish, and it is the earliest-known fish to possess a neck with the pectoral girdle separate from the skull.
The creature had a pelvis nearly the same size as its shoulder girdle and possessed about 45 pairs of ribs between its skull and hip region, though its vertebrae were not ossified.
While it possessed lobe-finned fish characteristics, its front fins included arm-like skeletal structures with a shoulder, elbow, and wrist similar to those of crocodiles.
This species holds the distinction of being the earliest-known fish to possess a neck, separating the pectoral girdle from the skull.
Indentations on the skull suggest the animal may have had primitive lungs in addition to gills.
The first fossils were discovered in 2004 on Ellesmere Island in Nunavut, Canada.
Edward B. Daeschler, Neil H. Shubin, and Farish A. Jenkins Jr. described the species Tiktaalik roseae in 2006, publishing their findings in the April 6, 2006 issue of Nature.
The specific name roseae honors an anonymous donor.
Researchers suggest that Tiktaalik likely flexed its proto-limbs on the riverbed and could push itself toward the shore for brief periods.
A 2014 discovery of a strongly built pelvic girdle indicated that the animal could move in shallow water and across mudflats.
During its time, flourishing deciduous plants shed leaves into warm, oxygen-poor shallows, attracting small prey that were difficult for larger fish to catch.
Tiktaalik is considered a transitional fossil between fish and tetrapods, comparable to Archaeopteryx's role between reptiles and birds.
It was originally described as a member of Elpistostegalia, belongs to the family Panderichthyidae, and is classified in the class Osteichthyes.
Tiktaalik lived during the Late Devonian period, specifically the Frasnian stage, between 382.31 and 372.15 million years ago.
When Tiktaalik existed, Ellesmere Island was part of the continent Laurentia, located near the equator with a warm climate.

It is debated whether Panderichthys is closer to tetrapods than Tiktaalik or if the similarity is due to convergence, as suggested by a 2008 paper by Boisvert et al. One hypothesis suggests that similarities between elpistostegalians and tetrapods result from convergent evolution rather than direct ancestry.
